slides.title:
It was made to
*clean walls*.
Kids made it a legend.
slides.sub:
A dying wallpaper cleaner.
Then 3 billion cans 👇

slides.title:
In Cincinnati, Kutol sells
a soft putty to *wipe coal
soot* off wallpaper.
slides.sub:
Noah McVicker created it at the request
of Kroger grocery stores (Wikipedia).

slides.title:
Homes switch from coal
to oil, gas and electricity.
*No soot, no customers.*
slides.sub:
Washable vinyl wallpaper finishes the job.
By the 1950s, sales collapse
(Smithsonian, Wikipedia).

slides.title:
A nursery school teacher,
Kay Zufall, has her kids
*sculpt with the cleaner*.
slides.sub:
She tells her brother-in-law Joe McVicker,
who is trying to save Kutol:
sell it as a toy (Smithsonian).

slides.title:
Same dough. New customer.
New name: *Play-Doh*.
slides.sub:
Name suggested by Kay and her husband.
Sold to schools first, then at Woodward
& Lothrop, a D.C. department store.

slides.title:
Captain Kangaroo talks
about it on TV in exchange
for *2 % of sales*.
slides.sub:
Sales soar in 1958: nearly $3 million
(Smithsonian, Wikipedia).

slides.title:
*cans sold* since 1956.
General Mills buys it for
$3 million in 1965.
slides.sub:
Hasbro owns it since 1991. Smithsonian,
citing Fortune: 3 billion+ cans.

slides.title: It's a tale of technological obsolescence *with a happy ending.*
slides.author:
Christopher Bensch, VP of collections,
The Strong National Museum of Play
(Smithsonian)

slides.title:
Your product may be
sold to *the wrong
customer*.
slides.sub:
Play-Doh didn't change. Its buyer did.
